qs.q: A 3-year-old child with a large, unrepaired ventricular septal defect develops Eisenmenger's syndrome. What primary physiological alteration characterizes this complication?
o: Spontaneous closure of the septal defect with resolution of heart failure
Marked reduction in pulmonary vascular resistance elevating the Qp:Qs ratio
Severe systemic hypotension driven by excessive peripheral afterload drop
Reversal of the shunt to right-to-left causing progressive central cyanosis
qs.e: Eisenmenger's syndrome occurs when chronic left-to-right shunting causes severe pulmonary vascular disease and pulmonary hypertension, eventually reversing the shunt to right-to-left. This process involves irreversible pulmonary vascular remodeling rather than a drop in resistance or spontaneous defect closure.

qs.q: Surgical closure of a complete ventricular septal defect is usually performed before what age to prevent Eisenmenger syndrome?
qs.e: Early repair (<6 months) avoids the development of Eisenmenger. Delaying beyond 1 year increases the risk.

qs.q: What is the definitive, appropriate surgical management for a child with a very large ventricular septal defect (VSD)?
o: Close monitoring for possible spontaneous closure
Palliative care provided for inoperable condition
Open‑heart patch closure using cardiopulmonary bypass
Primary suture repair performed under tension
qs.e: Very large VSDs require open-heart surgery with patch closure under cardiopulmonary bypass to prevent complications like heart failure and pulmonary hypertension. Monitoring closely is reserved for small, restrictive defects that have a high likelihood of spontaneous closure.

qs.q: A 3-year-old with a ventricular septal defect (VSD) initially had left-to-right shunting. One year later, the child presents with cyanosis and right-to-left shunting. What is this phenomenon called?
qs.e: The reversal of shunt direction from left-to-right to right-to-left in a long-standing VSD is known as Eisenmenger syndrome. Cor pulmonale refers to right heart failure, not the shunt reversal itself.

qs.q: A 6-month-old infant with a large, uncorrected ventricular septal defect undergoes echocardiography to assess cardiac remodeling. Which of the following sets of cardiac chambers is expected to show the greatest dilation?
qs.e: A left-to-right shunt at the ventricular level causes chronic volume overload resulting in dilation of the left atrium and left ventricle. In contrast, atrial-level shunts predominantly dilate the right-sided chambers.

qs.q: A 3-week-old infant with a moderate-sized ventricular septal defect has a normal physical examination without murmurs or signs of heart failure. Why do infants with this defect typically lack symptoms during the first few weeks of life?
o: The shunt orifice has not yet reached critical size
The ductus arteriosus temporarily masks the defect
Immediate closure of the foramen ovale limits flow
High fetal pulmonary vascular resistance limits the shunt
qs.e: High pulmonary vascular resistance in the first weeks of life limits the left-to-right shunt, delaying symptoms and murmurs until resistance drops around 4 to 8 weeks. Lower resistance would typically cause early manifestations of heart failure.

qs.q: Most ventricular septal defects (VSDs) occur in which part of the septum?
qs.e: The membranous part of the ventricular septum is the most common site for VSDs.
